module_title: General Organic Chemistry Basics & Structural Isomerism (Detailed Foundational)
introduction: General Organic Chemistry (GOC) is the absolute foundation of organic reactions. This level covers the mechanics of bond cleavage, the nature of attacking reagents, the fundamental permanent electronic displacement (Inductive Effect), and the classification of Structural Isomerism. Mastery here is non-negotiable for understanding organic reaction mechanisms.

core_concepts.title: Fission of a Covalent Bond
core_concepts.description:
Organic reactions initiate with bond breaking.
1. Homolytic Cleavage: Symmetrical breaking where each atom takes away one electron from the shared pair. This generates highly reactive, neutral species called Free Radicals. It is favored by high temperature, UV light, non-polar solvents, and peroxides (HELPR conditions).
2. Heterolytic Cleavage: Unsymmetrical breaking where the more electronegative atom takes both electrons of the shared pair. This generates charged species: a Carbocation (positive) and a Carbanion (negative). Favored by polar solvents and low temperatures.

core_concepts.title: Attacking Reagents: Electrophiles and Nucleophiles
core_concepts.description:
1. Electrophiles ($E^+$): Electron-deficient species that attack electron-rich centers. They are Lewis Acids. Examples include positively charged species ($H^+, NO_2^+, CH_3^+$) and neutral molecules with incomplete octets ($BF_3, AlCl_3$).
2. Nucleophiles ($Nu^-$): Electron-rich species that attack electron-deficient centers. They are Lewis Bases. Examples include negatively charged species ($OH^-, CN^-, Cl^-$) and neutral molecules with lone pairs ($H_2O, NH_3, R-OH$).

core_concepts.title: The Inductive Effect (I-Effect)
core_concepts.description:
A permanent, distance-dependent electronic effect involving the polarization of $\sigma$-bonds due to electronegativity differences. It propagates through a carbon chain but becomes almost negligible after the third carbon atom.
1. -I Effect (Electron Withdrawing): Groups more electronegative than hydrogen pull electron density. Order: $-NO_2 > -CN > -F > -Cl > -Br > -I > -OH > -OCH_3 > -C\equiv CH > -C_6H_5$.
2. +I Effect (Electron Donating): Groups less electronegative than hydrogen (usually alkyl groups) push electron density. Order: $-C(CH_3)_3 > -CH(CH_3)_2 > -CH_2CH_3 > -CH_3$.

core_concepts.title: Structural Isomerism
core_concepts.description:
Compounds having the same molecular formula but different structural connectivity.
1. Chain Isomerism: Difference in the carbon skeleton (straight vs. branched, e.g., n-butane and isobutane).
2. Position Isomerism: Difference in the position of a functional group, multiple bond, or substituent on the main chain (e.g., 1-propanol and 2-propanol).
3. Functional Isomerism: Different functional groups altogether (e.g., Alcohols and Ethers; Aldehydes and Ketones).
4. Metamerism: Difference in the alkyl chains attached on either side of a polyvalent functional group (like -O-, -S-, -NH-, -CO-). Example: Diethyl ether and Methyl propyl ether.

important_entities.name: Tautomerism (Keto-Enol)
important_entities.key_fact: A dynamic dynamic equilibrium between two structural isomers migrating a proton (alpha-hydrogen) and shifting a pi bond.
important_entities.significance: The most common form is Keto-Enol tautomerism. The Keto form ($>C=O$) is generally far more thermodynamically stable than the Enol form ($>C=C-OH$) due to the higher bond energy of the $C=O$ double bond compared to the $C=C$ bond. However, extensive hydrogen bonding or aromaticity can sometimes make the enol form exceptionally stable (e.g., Phenol).

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: A pervasive student trap. Tautomerism involves the actual physical migration of an ATOM (usually a proton) and changing the hybridization of carbon atoms, resulting in two distinct, separable chemical species in equilibrium. Resonance involves ONLY the hypothetical shifting of $\pi$-electrons or lone pairs; no atoms ever move, and the canonical forms do not exist in reality.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation:
To quickly identify functional isomer sets that share identical general formulas:
- Alcohols and Ethers ($C_nH_{2n+2}O$)
- Aldehydes and Ketones ($C_nH_{2n}O$)
- Carboxylic Acids and Esters ($C_nH_{2n}O_2$)

exam_strategy_tips: When asked to count the total number of structural isomers for a given molecular formula (e.g., $C_6H_{14}$), always calculate the Degree of Unsaturation (Double Bond Equivalent) first. $DU = C + 1 - \frac{H}{2} + \frac{N}{2} - \frac{X}{2}$. If $DU=0$, only alkanes/ethers/alcohols are possible. If $DU=1$, expect one double bond or one ring.
